Thirty kilometres from the nearest town, the fishing hamlet of Kolavi depended entirely on the morning catch for its income, but for years nearly a third of that catch rotted before it ever reached the market. The village had no electricity supply reliable enough to run refrigeration, and the nearest ice factory was three hours away by road. By the time boats returned at noon and traders finished bargaining, much of the fish had already begun to spoil in the afternoon heat. Ravi Oberoi, who had taken over as secretary of the local fishermen's cooperative two years earlier, had watched this waste erode the community's earnings season after season. Rather than wait for the state electricity board to extend its lines to Kolavi, he proposed a simpler fix: a set of insulated bamboo-and-thermocol ice boxes, cooled overnight using ice brought in bulk on the cooperative's only truck, and packed with sawdust to slow the melt through the following day. Each box could hold enough fish for a dozen households and kept the catch fresh for nearly ten hours longer than the open baskets the fishermen had used before. The cooperative pooled a small fund to build twenty such boxes in the first month. Within a single fishing season, spoilage losses fell from roughly a third of the catch to under a tenth, and household earnings from the fish trade rose noticeably enough that several families who had considered leaving the trade decided to stay. Traders who once discounted Kolavi's fish for its inconsistent freshness began offering prices closer to those paid at the main town market. Oberoi was careful to gauge the boxes' performance before scaling up, keeping a handwritten log of ice consumption and spoilage for every batch, and adjusting the sawdust packing whenever the numbers slipped. The cooperative now trains new members on the system as soon as they join, and box-building has become a small skill in its own right within the village. Word of Kolavi's ice boxes travelled quickly along the coast, and within a year, three neighbouring hamlets facing the same lack of ____________ had built their own versions of the design, adapting the box size to their own catch volumes.
